title: What Berklee gave him: jam sessions, Phil Wilson and writing
summary: He credits Berklee's night jam sessions, trombonist Phil Wilson who got him a Buddy Rich gig, and arranging teachers.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: What did you gain from Berklee?

Berklee was great. I mean I’ll be honest, and this is not a criticism of Berklee, the best I got was the jam sessions at night and stuff, after school and stuff. I played with all — I mean I played really out to lunch, avante garde stuff, which I still like a lot of that because it’s — like for me “Heart and Soul,” if it’s in there it’s great. The form doesn’t matter to me so much. I love like what we’re doing up here with the Harlem Blues and Jazz Band. But and in the classes I was just starting to write music, I loved writing music, I loved writing songs and stuff. I had Phil Wilson, the trombone player who played with Woody Herman, and great teacher, great. I mean he taught great but he was also, probably even more than Sonny, like the kind of guy you stand next to and like you learn so much just playing with him. And a couple of people really benefit every year, I mean he picked on me. He decided that he was going to help me man. Before I even knew what this expression meant, like he would yell across the lobby of the school and he said, “Hey Art, man, when are you going to start playing with some balls?” And I didn’t even know what it meant. Balls? I don’t think I knew. And he was like that. And he got me a gig with Buddy Rich for like 2-1/2 weeks when one of the guys had to leave before the new guy came in. And he was great. And I had arranging class with him. I had a great arranging teacher named Bob Chestnut. And not a well known name but he really was brilliant to work with. There was a guy Dean Earl there, he used to play piano with Charlie Parker and he’s on wire recordings with Charlie. So just the environment, it really got me into writing, I studied composition there. That was very helpful. So anyway but Phil has been a dear friend for years, and we don’t talk for years and then we’ll talk again. When I got the gig with Duke his reaction was like, “Son-of-a-bitch, I always wanted that gig, but I’m glad you got it, man.” Like that. Because he got this bass player on the gig, Paul Concella was his name, in the late 60s, who really could write like Duke who really had a sense of that, not exactly, but, you know. But that’s the school was like that. I mean when I was in high school I never thought I couldn’t do this. I had no idea © Fillius Jazz Archive -11-
